title: Go: From Zero to Backend
summary: A guided, hands-on course in Go that takes you from your very first line of code to the ideas that power real backend services. You read a short concept, build muscle memory by typing small, complete programs with the tutor — every line explained — and then apply what you learned in a graded challenge whose hidden tests decide correctness. Twenty-six units of steadily rising difficulty: printing with fmt, variables and types, control flow, loops, functions with multiple returns, your own structs and methods, interfaces, slices and maps, error handling, and the Go module system (go get); an intermediate database track built on SQLite through database/sql and the pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite driver — connecting and querying, transactions, the connection pool and WAL mode, the N+1 query problem, pagination, and indexes with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; then an advanced concurrency track — goroutines and WaitGroups, channels, select with timeouts, and shared state with mutexes and worker pools; and a data structures & algorithms track: stacks and queues, linked lists, maps and sets, binary search trees, sorting and searching, and recursion with dynamic programming. Almost everything runs on the standard library; two exercises teach you how to pull in and run an external package the way every real Go project does. No prior Go needed.

units.title: Hello & fmt
units.intro:
Your very first steps in Go: what a program is, how to print to the screen with
the `fmt` package, and how the compiler turns your text into a running binary. By
the end you will write a tiny greeting function and let the hidden tests check it.

steps.title: What a Go program is
steps.intro:
Before you write anything, picture what a computer actually does: it loads a
compiled program into memory and executes machine instructions one after another.
A program needs one agreed place to begin — in Go that place is the function
`main`, inside the special `package main`. The Go toolchain compiles your source
into a native binary; when you run it, the operating system hands control to
`main`, and anything you print travels to **standard output**, which the terminal
shows on screen.
steps.body:
## A program starts at `main`

Every runnable Go program lives in **`package main`** and begins at a function
called **`main`**. Think of `main` as the front door: when you run the program,
Go walks in through `main` and does, top to bottom, whatever it finds there.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, Go!")
}
```

Four things to notice:

- **`package main`** marks this file as a buildable command (not a library).
- **`import "fmt"`** pulls in the standard-library `fmt` package, which formats
  and prints text.
- **`func main() { ... }`** declares the entry point; the `{ }` hold its body.
- **`fmt.Println(...)`** prints a line of text, then a newline, to standard output.

You compile and run a single-file program with **`go run .`**. In the next steps
you will type small, complete programs yourself; when your code matches the
target, the tutor runs it so you can see the output.

steps.title: Print your first line
steps.intro:
This drill cements the one skeleton every Go program shares. `fmt.Println` writes
your text to standard output and adds a trailing newline. There is no loop and no
branching here — just the entry point `main` and a single write to the screen.
steps.prompt:
Type the classic first program. It prints a single line and stops.

**Why:** this cements the shape every Go program shares — `package main`, an
`import`, and a `main` that writes one line. Reproduce it exactly.
line_comments: Declares this file as part of `package main` — the special package that builds a runnable command.
Imports the standard-library `fmt` package, which formats and prints text.
Declares `main`, the function Go runs first; `{` opens its body.
Prints the text followed by a newline to standard output.
Closes the body of `main`; when execution reaches here the program ends.
steps.explanation:
That is a complete Go program. Go entered `main`, ran the one `fmt.Println`,
printed `Hello, Go!`, and then `main` ended — so the program finished. Every
program you write grows from exactly this skeleton.

steps.title: Format with Printf
steps.intro:
`fmt.Println` prints values as-is; `fmt.Printf` lets you build a formatted string
with **verbs**: `%s` for a string, `%d` for an integer. Unlike `Println`, `Printf`
does not add a newline for you, so you write `\n` yourself where you want one.
steps.prompt:
Use `fmt.Printf` with the `%s` and `%d` verbs to interpolate a name and a number
into one line. Note the explicit `\n` at the end.
line_comments: Declares `name` and infers its type (string) with the short form `:=`.
`Printf` fills `%s` with `name` and `%d` with `15`; `\n` ends the line.
steps.explanation:
`Printf` is the workhorse of formatted output: each verb (`%s`, `%d`, ...) is
replaced, left to right, by the matching argument. Because `Printf` prints exactly
what you give it, you control the newline with `\n`.

steps.title: Implement Greet
steps.intro:
Now you apply what you learned. In Go, strings join with the `+` operator, and a
function declares what it returns after its parameter list. Your function takes a
`string` and returns a new `string`. Hidden tests, not the screen, decide
correctness.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `Greet`:

```go
func Greet(name string) string { ... }
```

It takes a name and returns a string that reads `Hello, {name}!`.

Examples:

- `Greet("World")` → `"Hello, World!"`
- `Greet("Go")` → `"Hello, Go!"`

**Hint:** build the result by joining strings with `+`.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Joining strings copies the fixed text `Hello, ` and `!` plus the `n` characters of
`name` into a fresh string. Both the work and the memory grow in direct proportion
to the length of `name`, so the time is **O(n)** and the space is **O(n)**, where
`n` is the length of the name. There is no hidden loop — a single pass builds the
result once.

units.title: Variables & types
units.intro:
Every value in Go has a **type** the compiler tracks for you: whole numbers
(`int`), real numbers (`float64`), text (`string`), truth values (`bool`). You
will meet the two ways to declare a variable (`var` and the short `:=`) and see
why Go makes you convert between numeric types on purpose.

steps.title: Values, types and declarations
steps.intro:
A variable is a named box in memory holding a value of a fixed type. Go is
statically typed: the type is known at compile time, which lets the compiler catch
mistakes before the program ever runs.
steps.body:
## Two ways to declare

```go
var age int = 15   // explicit type
city := "Luanda"   // short form: type inferred as string
```

- **`var name type = value`** states the type explicitly.
- **`name := value`** is the short form (only inside functions); Go **infers** the
  type from the value.

Go's basic types include `int`, `float64`, `bool`, and `string`. Unlike some
languages, Go will **not** silently mix numeric types: to multiply an `int` by a
`float64` you must convert, e.g. `float64(count) * price`. That explicitness
prevents a whole class of rounding bugs.

steps.title: Declare with var and :=
steps.intro:
Both declaration forms store a typed value. `var age int = 15` is explicit; the
short `city := "Luanda"` infers `string`. Printing several values with `Println`
separates them with spaces.
steps.prompt: Declare one variable with `var` and one with `:=`, then print them.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var age int = 15
    city := "Luanda"
    fmt.Println(age, city)
}
line_comments: Declares `age` as an `int` with the explicit `var` form.
Declares `city` with the short `:=` form; its type is inferred as string.
Prints both values, separated by a space.
steps.explanation:
`var` and `:=` both create a typed variable — `:=` just lets the compiler infer
the type. Inside functions the short form is the idiomatic choice.

steps.title: Convert between number types
steps.intro:
Go will not mix an `int` and a `float64` automatically. To multiply them you
convert the `int` with `float64(...)` first. This drill shows that explicit
conversion.
steps.prompt:
Multiply an integer count by a floating-point price. Convert the `int` to
`float64` before the multiplication.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    count := 7
    price := 2.5
    total := float64(count) * price
    fmt.Println("Total:", total)
}
line_comments: `price` is inferred as `float64` because it has a decimal point.
Converts `count` to `float64` so the multiplication type-checks.
Prints a label and the computed total.
steps.explanation:
The compiler rejects `count * price` because the types differ. `float64(count)`
makes the conversion explicit and the intent obvious — Go never guesses for you.

steps.title: Implement CelsiusToFahrenheit
steps.intro:
Apply numeric types and arithmetic. The formula is `F = C * 9/5 + 32`. Because you
work entirely in `float64`, no conversion is needed inside the function — the
caller passes a `float64` and you return one.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `CelsiusToFahrenheit`:

```go
func CelsiusToFahrenheit(c float64) float64 { ... }
```

It converts a temperature in Celsius to Fahrenheit using `F = C * 9/5 + 32`.

Examples:

- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(0)` → `32`
- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(100)` → `212`
- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(-40)` → `-40`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations — one multiply, one
divide, one add — regardless of the input value. There is no loop and no allocation
that grows with the input, so both the time and the space are **O(1)** (constant).

units.title: Control flow (if / switch)
units.intro:
Programs make decisions. You will use `if`/`else` to branch on a boolean condition
and `switch` to pick cleanly among several cases. By the end you classify a number
in a graded challenge.

steps.title: Branching with if and switch
steps.intro:
A branch lets the program take one path or another depending on a condition
evaluated at run time. Go's `if` needs no parentheses around the condition, and
its `switch` does not fall through by default — each case stands alone.
steps.body:
## `if` / `else`

```go
if n%2 == 0 {
    fmt.Println("even")
} else {
    fmt.Println("odd")
}
```

The condition must be a `bool`. No parentheses are required; the braces are.

## `switch`

```go
switch day {
case 1:
    fmt.Println("Monday")
case 3:
    fmt.Println("Wednesday")
default:
    fmt.Println("Other")
}
```

Unlike C, Go does **not** fall through from one case to the next, so you rarely
need `break`. A `switch` with many cases reads far more clearly than a long chain
of `else if`.

steps.title: Branch with if/else
steps.intro:
`%` is the remainder operator. `n%2 == 0` is true exactly when `n` is even, so this
`if`/`else` prints one word or the other.
steps.prompt: Use `if`/`else` and the `%` operator to print whether a number is even or odd.
line_comments: If the remainder of `n` divided by 2 is zero, `n` is even.
Prints `odd` when `n` is not divisible by 2.
steps.explanation:
The condition `n%2 == 0` is a `bool`; Go runs the matching block and skips the
other. Change `n` and the branch taken changes with it.

steps.title: Choose with switch
steps.intro:
`switch` compares one value against several `case` labels and runs the first that
matches, with no fall-through. `default` handles everything else.
steps.prompt: Map a day number to a day name with a `switch`, including a `default`.
line_comments: Printed when `day == 3` — our value, so this runs.
steps.explanation:
Go runs exactly one matching case and then leaves the `switch` — no `break`
needed. Because `day` is 3, only `Wednesday` prints.

steps.title: Implement Sign
steps.intro:
Apply branching. You classify an integer as negative, zero, or positive and return
the matching word. Either an `if`/`else if`/`else` chain or a `switch` works.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `Sign`:

```go
func Sign(n int) string { ... }
```

Return `"negative"` when `n < 0`, `"zero"` when `n == 0`, and `"positive"` when
`n > 0`.

Examples:

- `Sign(-5)` → `"negative"`
- `Sign(0)` → `"zero"`
- `Sign(42)` → `"positive"`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function checks at most two comparisons and returns — the number of operations
does not depend on how large `n` is. No loop, no allocation that grows with input,
so both time and space are **O(1)**.

units.title: Loops (for)
units.intro:
Repetition is where computers shine. Go has exactly one loop keyword — `for` — that
plays every role: counting loop, while-style loop, and range loop over a collection.
By the end you sum the numbers up to `n` in a graded challenge.

steps.title: The one loop: for
steps.intro:
A loop repeats a block while a condition holds. Go unifies all looping into the
single keyword `for`, so there is less to remember and one shape to master.
steps.body:
## Three shapes, one keyword

```go
for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {   // classic counter: init; condition; post
    sum += i
}

for condition {             // while-style
    // ...
}

for i, v := range nums {    // range over a slice/map/string
    fmt.Println(i, v)
}
```

- The **classic** form has three parts: an initializer, a condition, and a
  post-statement (`i++`).
- Drop the init and post to get a **while** loop.
- **`range`** walks a collection, handing you the index and the value each turn.

Loop cost matters: a single `for` over `n` items is **O(n)**; a loop inside a loop
is **O(n²)**. You will meet that idea again when complexity is graded.

steps.title: Count with a for loop
steps.intro:
The classic three-part `for` runs its body once per value of `i`, from 1 through 5,
accumulating the running total in `sum`.
steps.prompt: Add the numbers 1 through 5 with a classic `for` loop and print the total.
line_comments: Starts the running total at zero.
Loops `i` from 1 while `i <= 5`, adding 1 each turn (`i++`).
Adds the current `i` to `sum` (`+=` means `sum = sum + i`).
steps.explanation:
The loop body runs five times, once for each `i` in 1..5, and `sum` grows to 15.
One pass over `n` items is linear — **O(n)** work.

steps.title: Walk a slice with range
steps.intro:
`range` over a slice yields the index and the value on each turn. It is the
idiomatic way to visit every element without managing an index by hand.
steps.prompt: Use `for ... range` to print the index and value of each item in a slice.
line_comments: Creates a slice of three integers.
`range` yields each index `i` and value `v` in turn.
Prints the index and the value side by side.
steps.explanation:
`range` is the cleanest way to visit every element. Each turn binds `i` to the
position and `v` to a copy of the value at that position.

steps.title: Implement SumTo
steps.intro:
Apply looping. You add every integer from 1 to `n`. A single `for` loop does it in
one linear pass; the closed-form `n*(n+1)/2` would do it in constant time, but a
loop is the point of this unit.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SumTo`:

```go
func SumTo(n int) int { ... }
```

Return the sum `1 + 2 + ... + n`. For `n <= 0`, return `0`.

Examples:

- `SumTo(5)` → `15`
- `SumTo(1)` → `1`
- `SumTo(0)` → `0`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The loop runs `n` times, doing constant work per turn, so the running time grows
linearly with `n` — **O(n)**. Only the single accumulator `total` is stored,
regardless of `n`, so the extra space is **O(1)**.

units.title: Functions & multiple returns
units.intro:
Functions package a piece of work behind a name so you can call it anywhere. Go
functions can return **several values at once** — the idiom behind both `(result,
error)` and small helpers like min/max. By the end you return a quotient and a
remainder together.

steps.title: Declaring and returning
steps.intro:
A function has a name, a list of typed parameters, a list of result types, and a
body. Go's ability to return more than one value is used everywhere in the
standard library.

steps.title: Write and call a function
steps.intro:
`square` takes one `int` and returns one `int`. `main` calls it and prints the
result. Declaring a helper above `main` keeps each piece small and named.
steps.prompt: Define a `square` function and call it from `main`.
line_comments: Declares `square`, taking an `int` and returning an `int`.
Returns the parameter multiplied by itself.
Calls `square(6)` and prints the returned value, 36.
steps.explanation:
A function is a reusable, named block. `square` hides the detail `x * x` behind a
meaningful name you can call as often as you like.

steps.title: Return two values
steps.intro:
`minMax` returns two `int`s. The caller destructures them with `lo, hi := ...`.
This two-value return is the shape Go uses for `(result, error)` throughout the
standard library.
steps.prompt:
Write a `minMax` that returns the smaller then the larger of two numbers, and
unpack both results in `main`.
line_comments: Declares `minMax` returning two `int`s (the result types in parentheses).
If `a` is already the smaller, return it first.
Otherwise `b` is smaller, so return `b` then `a`.
Calls `minMax` and unpacks both results into `lo` and `hi`.
Prints the smaller then the larger: 3 8.
steps.explanation:
Multiple return values let one call hand back everything the caller needs. This is
exactly how `(value, error)` works later — two values from one function.

steps.title: Implement DivMod
steps.intro:
Apply multiple returns. Integer division in Go uses `/` for the quotient and `%`
for the remainder. You return both in one call — the quotient first, the remainder
second.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `DivMod`:

```go
func DivMod(a, b int) (int, int) { ... }
```

Return the integer quotient `a / b` and the remainder `a % b`, in that order.

Examples:

- `DivMod(17, 5)` → `(3, 2)`
- `DivMod(10, 2)` → `(5, 0)`

(You may assume `b` is not zero — division by zero comes up in the errors unit.)

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function performs two constant-time arithmetic operations — one division and
one remainder — no matter how large the inputs are. No loops and no growing
allocation, so both time and space are **O(1)**.

units.title: Structs & methods
units.intro:
Real programs model things — a user, a rectangle, a request. A **struct** groups
related fields into one named type, and a **method** attaches behaviour to that
type. By the end you give a `Rectangle` an `Area` method.

steps.title: Your own types
steps.intro:
A struct is a composite type: several typed fields bundled under one name. A method
is a function with a **receiver** — the value it acts on — written just before the
name. Together they are how Go models data and the behaviour that belongs with it.
steps.body:
## Struct + method

```go
type Rectangle struct {
    Width  float64
    Height float64
}

func (r Rectangle) Area() float64 {
    return r.Width * r.Height
}
```

- **`type Name struct { ... }`** declares a new type with named fields.
- Create a value with `Rectangle{Width: 3, Height: 4}` and read a field with
  `r.Width`.
- **`func (r Rectangle) Area() float64`** adds a method; `r` is the receiver, the
  specific rectangle the method runs on. Call it with `r.Area()`.

Capitalised names (`Width`, `Area`) are **exported** — visible from other packages;
lowercase names are private to the package. That single rule is Go's whole access
model.

steps.title: Define and use a struct
steps.intro:
`Point` groups two `int` fields. You build one with a composite literal and read
its fields with the dot operator.
steps.prompt: Define a `Point` struct with `X` and `Y`, create one, and print its fields.
line_comments: Reads the fields with the dot operator and prints them.
steps.explanation:
A struct bundles related values under one name. Building with named fields
(`X: 3, Y: 4`) makes the code self-documenting.

steps.title: Attach a method
steps.intro:
A method is a function with a receiver. `Celsius` is a named type over `float64`,
and `ToFahrenheit` is a method on it — behaviour that travels with the value.
steps.prompt: Give a `Celsius` type a `ToFahrenheit` method and call it.
line_comments: Declares `Celsius` as a named type over `float64`.
Defines a method with receiver `c Celsius` returning a `float64`.
Converts the receiver and applies the conversion formula.
Calls the method on it and prints 212.
steps.explanation:
A method ties behaviour to a type. `t.ToFahrenheit()` reads as "ask this
temperature for its Fahrenheit value" — the receiver `c` is `t`.

steps.title: Implement Rectangle.Area
steps.intro:
Apply structs and methods. Define a `Rectangle` type with `Width` and `Height`,
and an `Area` method that returns their product. The hidden tests build rectangles
and call `Area`.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Define a `Rectangle` struct and an `Area` method:

```go
type Rectangle struct {
    Width  float64
    Height float64
}

func (r Rectangle) Area() float64 { ... }
```

`Area` returns `Width * Height`.

Examples:

- `Rectangle{Width: 3, Height: 4}.Area()` → `12`
- `Rectangle{Width: 2.5, Height: 2}.Area()` → `5`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
`Area` multiplies two fields once — a single constant-time operation regardless of
the values. No loops and no allocation that grows with input, so both time and
space are **O(1)**.

units.title: Interfaces
units.intro:
An **interface** names a set of methods. Any type that has those methods satisfies
the interface automatically — no `implements` keyword. This is how Go writes code
that works with many types at once. By the end you total the area of a mixed list
of shapes.

steps.title: Behaviour, not data
steps.intro:
An interface describes what a value can **do**, not what it **is**. If a type has
the right methods, it fits the interface implicitly — this decoupling is the heart
of Go's approach to polymorphism.

steps.title: Define and satisfy an interface
steps.intro:
`Greeter` requires one method, `Greet`. `Robot` has it, so a `Robot` value can be
stored in a `Greeter` variable — satisfaction is implicit.
steps.prompt:
Declare a `Greeter` interface, implement it with a `Robot`, and call it through
the interface.
line_comments: ...which requires one method: `Greet` returning a string.
Gives `Robot` a `Greet` method, so it satisfies `Greeter`.
Stores a `Robot` in a `Greeter` variable — allowed because it has `Greet`.
Calls the method through the interface.
steps.explanation:
`Robot` never declares that it implements `Greeter`; having the `Greet` method is
enough. That implicit satisfaction is what makes Go interfaces so flexible.

steps.title: One loop, many types
steps.intro:
Two different types, `Dog` and `Cat`, each implement `Stringer`. A slice of
`Stringer` holds both, and one loop calls `String` on every element regardless of
its concrete type.
steps.prompt:
Put two different types that share a method into one interface slice, then loop
over them.
line_comments: Builds a slice holding both a `Dog` and a `Cat` as `Stringer`s.
Loops over each element, ignoring the index with `_`.
Calls `String` through the interface — the right method runs for each type.
steps.explanation:
The slice stores different concrete types behind one interface. The loop does not
care which is which — it just asks each for its `String`, and Go dispatches to the
correct method.

steps.title: Implement TotalArea
steps.intro:
Apply interfaces. Define a `Shape` interface with an `Area` method, two concrete
shapes that satisfy it, and a `TotalArea` function that sums the areas of any
slice of shapes — one loop over the interface, whatever the concrete types.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Define a `Shape` interface and a function that totals areas:

```go
type Shape interface {
    Area() float64
}

func TotalArea(shapes []Shape) float64 { ... }
```

Also define two shapes that satisfy `Shape`:

- `Square{Side float64}` with `Area() = Side * Side`
- `Rect{Width, Height float64}` with `Area() = Width * Height`

`TotalArea` returns the sum of `Area()` over every shape in the slice.

Example:

- `TotalArea([]Shape{Square{Side: 2}, Rect{Width: 3, Height: 4}})` → `16`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
`TotalArea` visits each of the `n` shapes once, calling a constant-time `Area` and
adding it to a running total, so the time is **O(n)**. Only the single accumulator
is stored, independent of `n`, so the extra space is **O(1)**.

units.title: Slices & maps
units.intro:
Two collections power almost every Go program: the **slice** (a growable, ordered
list) and the **map** (a key→value lookup table). By the end you count how many
times each word appears — a tiny search index.

steps.title: Slices and maps
steps.intro:
A slice is a view over a contiguous, growable array of elements of one type. A map
stores key→value pairs with average constant-time lookup via hashing. Between them
they cover ordered lists and keyed lookups.
steps.body:
## Slice

```go
nums := []int{1, 2, 3}
nums = append(nums, 4)   // grows the slice
fmt.Println(len(nums))   // 4
```

`append` returns a (possibly new) slice, so you assign it back. `len` reports the
length.

## Map

```go
ages := map[string]int{"Ana": 30}
ages["Bo"] = 25             // insert
fmt.Println(ages["Ana"])    // 30

n, ok := ages["Zed"]        // ok is false when the key is absent
```

A map lookup is **O(1)** on average — that is why maps are the go-to tool for
counting, grouping, and de-duplicating. The comma-ok form (`n, ok := m[k]`) tells
you whether the key existed.

steps.title: Grow a slice with append
steps.intro:
`append` adds an element and returns the resulting slice, which you store back into
`nums`. `len` reports how many elements it now holds.
steps.prompt: Create a slice, append to it, and print the slice and its length.
line_comments: Creates a slice of three integers.
Appends a 4; `append` returns the new slice, assigned back to `nums`.
Prints the slice and its length (4).
steps.explanation:
Slices grow with `append`, which may allocate a bigger backing array and return a
new slice header — so you always assign the result back.

steps.title: Look things up with a map
steps.intro:
A map associates keys with values. You create one with a literal, insert with
`m[key] = value`, and read with `m[key]`.
steps.prompt: Create a map from names to ages, insert a new pair, and print two values.
line_comments: Creates a map from string keys to int values, with one pair.
Inserts a second pair by assigning to a new key.
Looks up both keys and prints their values.
steps.explanation:
Maps give you average constant-time lookup by key — the right tool whenever you
need to find a value by name rather than by position.

steps.title: Implement WordCount
steps.intro:
Apply slices and maps together. You walk a slice of words once and tally each word
in a map — the core of every search index and histogram. One linear pass does it.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `WordCount`:

```go
func WordCount(words []string) map[string]int { ... }
```

Return a map from each distinct word to the number of times it appears in the
slice.

Examples:

- `WordCount([]string{"a", "b", "a"})` → `{"a": 2, "b": 1}`
- `WordCount(nil)` → `{}` (an empty, non-nil map)

**Hint:** start with `counts := make(map[string]int)` and do `counts[w]++` for
each word.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function makes one pass over the `n` words, doing an average constant-time map
update per word, so the time is **O(n)**. The map stores one entry per distinct
word, so the space is **O(k)** where `k` is the number of distinct words
(`k <= n`).

units.title: Errors
units.intro:
Go has no exceptions. Instead, a function that can fail returns an `error` as its
last result, and the caller checks it. You will use `errors.New`, `fmt.Errorf` with
`%w`, and the `err != nil` pattern. By the end you divide safely, returning an error
on divide-by-zero.

steps.title: Errors are values
steps.intro:
In Go an error is just a value that implements the `error` interface (one method,
`Error() string`). Returning errors instead of throwing them makes every failure
path explicit and visible in the code.

steps.title: Return an error
steps.intro:
`check` returns an `error`: a real error value on bad input, or `nil` on success.
`main` prints whatever came back.
steps.prompt: Write a function that returns an error for a negative age, and `nil` otherwise.
line_comments: ...return a new error describing the problem.
Calls `check` with a bad value and keeps the returned error.
steps.explanation:
An error is an ordinary return value. `errors.New` makes one; `nil` means success.
The caller decides what to do by checking the value.

steps.title: Wrap an error with %w
steps.intro:
`fmt.Errorf` with `%w` adds context while keeping the original error inside, so
`errors.Is` can still match it. A package-level sentinel error (`ErrEmpty`) is the
value you compare against.
steps.prompt:
Wrap a sentinel error with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", ...)` and check it with
`errors.Is`.
line_comments: Declares a package-level sentinel error to compare against.
...wrap the sentinel with extra context using `%w`.
Prints the wrapped error and whether `errors.Is` still matches the sentinel.
steps.explanation:
`%w` wraps an error so context piles up without losing the original. `errors.Is`
unwraps the chain and reports `true` because `ErrEmpty` is still in there.

steps.title: Implement SafeDivide
steps.intro:
Apply the error pattern. You return `(quotient, error)`: the real quotient and a
`nil` error on success, or a zero quotient and a non-nil error when the divisor is
zero. This is the canonical Go signature for an operation that can fail.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SafeDivide`:

```go
func SafeDivide(a, b int) (int, error) { ... }
```

Return `(a/b, nil)` normally. When `b == 0`, return `(0, <some error>)` — build the
error with `errors.New`.

Examples:

- `SafeDivide(10, 2)` → `(5, nil)`
- `SafeDivide(1, 0)` → `(0, <non-nil error>)`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function does one comparison and at most one division — a fixed amount of work
regardless of the operands. No loops and no allocation that grows with input, so
both time and space are **O(1)**.

units.title: Goroutines, channels & packages
units.intro:
The two things real Go backends lean on most: lightweight **concurrency**
(goroutines, channels, `sync.WaitGroup`) and the **module system** that pulls in
other people's code with `go get`. You will run concurrent work, coordinate it, use
two popular external packages, and finish by summing a slice concurrently.

steps.title: Goroutines, channels, and go get
steps.intro:
A goroutine is a function running concurrently, scheduled by the Go runtime on top
of OS threads — cheap enough to launch thousands. Channels pass values safely
between goroutines. And when your program needs code it did not write, the module
system fetches it with `go get`.
steps.body:
## Goroutines & channels

```go
done := make(chan string)   // a channel of strings
go func() {                 // launch a goroutine
    done <- "finished"      // send on the channel
}()
msg := <-done               // receive (blocks until a value arrives)
```

- **`go f()`** runs `f` concurrently and returns immediately.
- A **channel** (`make(chan T)`) is a typed pipe; `ch <- v` sends, `<-ch` receives.
- Receiving **blocks** until a value is ready, which is how goroutines synchronise.

## Waiting for many: sync.WaitGroup

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); work() }()
}
wg.Wait()   // blocks until all three call Done
```

## Pulling in packages with go get

Real services use libraries. You add one to your module and download it with:

```sh
go get github.com/google/uuid
```

Then `import "github.com/google/uuid"` and run with `go run .`. The toolchain
records the dependency in `go.mod` and its exact version in `go.sum`. The next two
drills do exactly this with two well-known packages — watch the tutor show you the
install command.

steps.title: Launch a goroutine, use a channel
steps.intro:
A goroutine runs the anonymous function concurrently; it sends a message on the
channel, and `main` blocks on the receive until that value arrives — a clean
hand-off between concurrent work and the main flow.
steps.prompt: Start a goroutine that sends a string on a channel, and receive it in `main`.
line_comments: Creates a channel that carries strings.
Launches a goroutine running an anonymous function.
Sends a value into the channel (blocks until someone receives).
Closes and immediately calls the anonymous function.
Receives from the channel — blocks until the goroutine sends.
steps.explanation:
The `go` keyword starts concurrent work; the channel both passes the value and
synchronises the two goroutines — `main` waits at `<-done` until the value is sent.

steps.title: Coordinate with sync.WaitGroup
steps.intro:
A `sync.WaitGroup` counts outstanding goroutines. Each `Add(1)` before launching,
each `Done()` as it finishes, and `Wait()` blocks until the count returns to zero —
so `main` does not exit before the workers do.
steps.prompt: Launch three goroutines and wait for all of them with a `sync.WaitGroup`.
line_comments: Declares a WaitGroup to track running goroutines.
Registers one more goroutine with the group.
Launches a goroutine, passing the loop value as `n`.
`defer` guarantees `Done` runs when the goroutine returns.
Closes and calls the goroutine with the current `i`.
Blocks until all three workers have called `Done`.
Prints a final line after everyone finished.
steps.explanation:
`Add`/`Done`/`Wait` are the counter that lets `main` wait for concurrent work.
Passing `i` as an argument gives each goroutine its own copy. Worker lines may print
in any order — that is concurrency.

steps.title: Use a package: google/uuid
steps.intro:
Time to use code you did not write. `github.com/google/uuid` generates universally
unique identifiers — the kind every backend stamps on a new record or request.
First install it with `go get`, then import and call it. The tutor shows the exact
install command above; the evaluator resolves the module for you with `go mod tidy`.
steps.prompt:
Install `github.com/google/uuid` with `go get`, then generate and print a new UUID.

Run it with `go run .` after installing.
line_comments: ...and the external package `github.com/google/uuid` (installed with go get).
Calls `uuid.New()` to generate a fresh random UUID.
Prints the UUID as a string.
steps.explanation:
This is the everyday Go workflow: `go get` records the dependency in `go.mod`, the
import names it, and `go run .` builds and runs. You just used third-party code the
same way every production service does.

steps.title: Use a package: rsc.io/quote
steps.intro:
A second, tiny package to drive the module workflow home. `rsc.io/quote` (by a Go
team member) just returns famous sayings — ideal for practising `go get` without
any setup. Install it, import it, and print one of Go's own proverbs.
steps.prompt:
Install `rsc.io/quote` with `go get`, then print the Go proverb it returns.

Run it with `go run .` after installing.
line_comments: ...and the external package `rsc.io/quote` (installed with go get).
Calls `quote.Go()`, which returns a well-known Go proverb.
steps.explanation:
Two `go get` commands, two external packages, the same three steps each time:
install, import, run. The module system makes reusing code routine — which is why
Go backends are so quick to assemble.

steps.title: Implement SumConcurrent
steps.intro:
Tie it together. You sum a slice of integers using concurrency: launch goroutines
that each report a partial result over a channel, then combine them. The answer must
be deterministic even though the work runs concurrently — the sum of a set does not
depend on the order you add it.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SumConcurrent`:

```go
func SumConcurrent(nums []int) int { ... }
```

Return the sum of all the integers in `nums`, computed with the help of goroutines
and a channel (or a `sync.WaitGroup`). The result must be correct and deterministic
regardless of goroutine scheduling.

Examples:

- `SumConcurrent([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})` → `15`
- `SumConcurrent(nil)` → `0`

**Hint:** send each number (or a partial sum) on a channel and add up everything
you receive. Addition is commutative, so order does not matter.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n` numbers is handled by one goroutine that sends on the channel, and
the collector receives `n` values, so the work is **O(n)**. The buffered channel
holds up to `n` pending values, so the extra space is **O(n)**. Because addition is
commutative, the total is the same no matter which goroutine is scheduled first,
which keeps the result deterministic.

units.title: Databases: connect & query
units.intro:
Real services keep their state in a database. Go talks to SQL databases through the
standard `database/sql` package plus a driver. Here you use SQLite with the pure-Go
driver `modernc.org/sqlite` (no C compiler needed): open a database, create a table,
insert rows with `?` placeholders, and read them back with `QueryRow` and `Query`.

steps.title: database/sql and a driver
steps.intro:
`database/sql` is a thin, driver-agnostic layer. You import a driver for its side
effect (a blank import) so it registers itself, then open a handle by the driver's
registered name.
steps.body:
## Open, exec, query

```go
import (
    "database/sql"

    _ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
defer db.Close()

db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)`)
db.Exec(`INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)`, 1, "Ana")

var n int
db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users`).Scan(&n)
```

- The **blank import** `_ "modernc.org/sqlite"` registers the driver named `sqlite`.
- **`sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")`** returns a `*sql.DB` handle — a pool, not a
  single connection.
- **`Exec`** runs statements that return no rows; **`?`** placeholders bind values
  safely (never build SQL by string concatenation).
- **`QueryRow(...).Scan(&n)`** reads exactly one row into Go variables.

For many rows, use `Query` and loop with `rows.Next()` / `rows.Scan(...)`, and always
`defer rows.Close()`.

steps.title: Open, create, count
steps.intro:
Open an in-memory SQLite database, create a table, insert one row, and count the
rows. The driver is registered by the blank import; `:memory:` is a throwaway
database that lives only while the program runs.
steps.prompt:
Open `:memory:`, create a table, insert a row with `?` placeholders, and print
`COUNT(*)`.
steps.target:

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)`, 1, "Ana")
	var n int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users`).Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println(n)

line_comments: ...plus the pure-Go `modernc.org/sqlite` driver, blank-imported so it registers itself under the name `sqlite`.
Opens an in-memory SQLite database; the driver name is `sqlite`.
Inserts one row; the `?` placeholders bind the values safely.
Runs `COUNT(*)` and scans the single result into `n`.
steps.explanation:
`sql.Open` hands you a pool; `Exec` runs statements; `QueryRow(...).Scan` reads one
value. Placeholders keep the values separate from the SQL text.

steps.title: QueryRow with a placeholder
steps.intro:
`QueryRow` plus a bound `?` fetches a single value for a single key — the everyday
lookup. Insert two people, then read one person's age back by name.
steps.prompt:
Insert two rows, then use `QueryRow(... WHERE name = ?, "Ana").Scan(&age)` and print
the age.

Creates a `people` table with a name and an age.
Inserts two rows in one statement; each `?` binds one value.
Will hold the age we look up.
Looks up Ana's age with a bound `?` and scans it into `age`.
steps.explanation:
A bound parameter (`?`) is matched positionally with the argument you pass after the
SQL. `Scan` copies the column into your Go variable.

steps.title: Loop over many rows
steps.intro:
When a query returns several rows you iterate with `rows.Next()` and `rows.Scan()`.
`ORDER BY` makes the output deterministic. Remember to `defer rows.Close()`.
steps.prompt:
Insert three numbers, `Query` them `ORDER BY x`, sum them in a `rows.Next()` loop,
and print the total.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE nums (x INTEGER)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO nums VALUES (10), (20), (30)`)

Runs a query that returns many rows, ordered for determinism.
Closes the row set when done.
Running total of the scanned values.
Advances to the next row until there are none.
steps.explanation:
`Query` returns a cursor; each `Next()` advances it and `Scan` reads the current row.
Ordering the query keeps the printed result stable run to run.

steps.title: Implement CountAdults
steps.intro:
Put the query pattern to work. You receive rows of `(name, age)` as `[][2]any`,
insert them into a table, and return how many people are adults — counted by SQL,
not by a Go loop.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `CountAdults`:

```go
func CountAdults(rows [][2]any) int { ... }
```

Each element is `[2]any{name, age}`. Open an in-memory database, create a table,
insert every row with `?` placeholders, and return `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE
age >= 18`.

Examples:

- `CountAdults([][2]any{{"Ana", 30}, {"Bo", 17}})` -> `1`
- `CountAdults(nil)` -> `0`

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n` input rows is inserted once, so the work and the stored rows both
grow linearly: **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space. The `COUNT(*)` with a `WHERE` runs
inside SQLite; the boundary `age >= 18` is handled by the database, not Go.

units.title: Transactions: all or nothing
units.intro:
A transaction groups several statements so they either all take effect or none do.
You use `db.Begin()` to start one, run statements on the returned `*sql.Tx`, then
`Commit()` to keep the changes or `Rollback()` to discard them. You will build a
money transfer that rolls back rather than leave an account negative.

steps.title: Begin, Commit, Rollback
steps.intro:
Without a transaction, each statement commits on its own — a crash halfway leaves
inconsistent data. A transaction makes a group of statements atomic.
steps.body:
## The transaction shape

```go
tx, err := db.Begin()
if err != nil {
    return err
}
tx.Exec(`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = 1`, amount)
tx.Exec(`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = 2`, amount)

if bad {
    tx.Rollback() // undo everything in this tx
    return nil
}
tx.Commit() // make it permanent
```

- **`db.Begin()`** returns a `*sql.Tx`; run your statements on `tx`, not `db`.
- **`tx.Commit()`** makes every change in the transaction permanent at once.
- **`tx.Rollback()`** throws the whole group away — the database looks as if nothing
  happened.
- A transfer is the classic example: debit and credit must both succeed, or neither.

steps.title: Commit keeps the change
steps.intro:
Begin a transaction, insert a row, and `Commit`. After committing, the row is really
there — the count is 1.
steps.prompt: Inside a transaction insert one row, `Commit`, then print `COUNT(*)`.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)`)
	tx, _ := db.Begin()
	tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)`)
	tx.Commit()
	var n int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t`).Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println(n)
}
line_comments: ...plus the pure-Go `modernc.org/sqlite` driver, blank-imported so it registers itself under the name `sqlite`.
Inserts a row inside the transaction.
Counts the rows after the commit.
Prints 1 — the committed row is there.
steps.explanation:
Statements run on the `*sql.Tx`. `Commit` publishes them; a later read on the `db`
handle sees the committed row.

steps.title: Rollback undoes the change
steps.intro:
Same insert, but call `Rollback` instead of `Commit`. The insert is discarded, so the
count is 0 — proof that nothing in a rolled-back transaction survives.
steps.prompt: Inside a transaction insert one row, `Rollback`, then print `COUNT(*)`.

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"

Inserts a row inside the transaction.
Rolls back, discarding everything the transaction did.
Counts the rows after the rollback.
Prints 0 — the rolled-back insert left no trace.

`Rollback` discards every change made since `Begin`. The row never becomes visible,
so the count stays at 0.

steps.title: Two updates, one commit
steps.intro:
A transfer is two updates that must land together. Debit one account and credit
another inside a single transaction, commit, and read the destination balance.
steps.prompt:
Seed two accounts, in one transaction move 40 from account 1 to account 2, commit,
and print account 2's balance.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE acct (id INTEGER, bal INTEGER)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100), (2, 0)`)
	tx, _ := db.Begin()
	tx.Exec(`UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 40 WHERE id = 1`)
	tx.Exec(`UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 40 WHERE id = 2`)
	tx.Commit()
	var b int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 2`).Scan(&b)

Seeds account 1 with 100 and account 2 with 0.
Begins a transaction so both updates land together.
Reads account 2's balance after the commit.
steps.explanation:
Both `UPDATE`s run inside the same transaction, so `Commit` applies them atomically.
Account 2 ends with the 40 that left account 1.

steps.title: Implement Transfer
steps.intro:
Make the transfer safe. Move `amount` from A to B inside one transaction; if either
balance would end up negative, roll the whole thing back and report the original
balances unchanged.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `Transfer`:

```go
func Transfer(a0, b0, amount int) (int, int) { ... }
```

Seed account A with `a0` and account B with `b0`. In ONE transaction, subtract
`amount` from A and add it to B. If either resulting balance is negative, `Rollback`
and return `(a0, b0)`. Otherwise `Commit` and return the new `(A, B)`.

Examples:

- `Transfer(100, 50, 30)` -> `(70, 80)`
- `Transfer(20, 0, 50)` -> `(20, 0)` (rolled back — A cannot go to -30)

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The work is a fixed number of statements regardless of the inputs, so both time and
space are **O(1)**. Atomicity comes from the transaction: on the overdraw path the
`Rollback` restores the opening balances, which is why the originals come back
unchanged.

units.title: WAL mode & the connection pool
units.intro:
`*sql.DB` is a pool of connections, not a single wire — safe to share across
goroutines. SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode lets readers and a writer work
concurrently. Here you turn on WAL, cap the pool with `SetMaxOpenConns`, and have
several goroutines insert through the shared pool to a deterministic total.

steps.title: A pool you can share
steps.intro:
`sql.Open` returns a pool. Goroutines can call it concurrently; the pool hands each
one a free connection. WAL mode improves read/write concurrency on SQLite.
steps.body:
## Pool and WAL

```go
db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:app.db")
db.SetMaxOpenConns(4) // at most 4 live connections

db.Exec(`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) // readers don't block the writer

var wg sync.WaitGroup
for w := 0; w < 4; w++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        db.Exec(`INSERT INTO nums VALUES (?)`, 1)
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
```

- **`*sql.DB` is safe for concurrent use** — share the one handle, never open a pool
  per goroutine.
- **`SetMaxOpenConns(n)`** bounds how many connections exist at once.
- **WAL** (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) needs a real file, not `:memory:`, and lets
  reads proceed while a write is in flight.
- A **busy timeout** makes a connection wait briefly for a lock instead of failing
  immediately — add it to the DSN so every pooled connection inherits it.

steps.title: Turn on WAL
steps.intro:
WAL mode needs a file-backed database, so this drill creates a temporary file. The
`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` statement both sets the mode and returns it, so you can
read it back.
steps.prompt:
Open a file-backed database and run `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`, scanning and printing
the mode it returns.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	dir, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "wal")
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:"+filepath.Join(dir, "w.db"))
	defer db.Close()
	var mode string
	db.QueryRow(`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`).Scan(&mode)

Opens a file-backed SQLite database under that directory.
Will hold the journal mode the PRAGMA reports back.
Switches the database to Write-Ahead Logging and reads the mode back.
Prints `wal`, confirming the mode is active.
steps.explanation:
WAL is a durable journalling mode, so it only works on a real file. The PRAGMA
returns the active mode, which prints as `wal`.

steps.title: Cap the pool
steps.intro:
`SetMaxOpenConns` bounds the pool. Insert a handful of rows through it and sum them
back — a warm-up before adding goroutines.
steps.prompt: Open a file-backed database, `SetMaxOpenConns(4)`, insert 1..5, and print the `SUM`.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	dir, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "pool")
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:"+filepath.Join(dir, "p.db"))
	defer db.Close()
	db.SetMaxOpenConns(4)
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE nums (x INTEGER)`)
	for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
		db.Exec(`INSERT INTO nums VALUES (?)`, i)

units.title: The N+1 query problem
units.intro:
A loop that runs one query per id is the N+1 anti-pattern: for N ids you pay N round
trips (plus the one that produced the ids). Folding them into a single `IN (...)`
query is dramatically faster. You will count the queries both ways and then return a
total using exactly one query.

steps.title: One query, not N
steps.intro:
Each database round trip has a cost. Doing one per item inside a loop multiplies that
cost by N. A single set-based query does the same work in one trip.
steps.body:
## N+1 vs a single query

```go
// N+1: one query per id (slow)
for _, id := range ids {
    db.QueryRow(`SELECT price FROM orders WHERE id = ?`, id).Scan(&p)
    total += p
}

// One query for all ids (fast)
db.QueryRow(`SELECT SUM(price) FROM orders WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)`).Scan(&total)
```

- The loop issues **N** separate queries — the classic N+1 pattern.
- The set-based version makes **one** round trip with an `IN (...)` list.
- Build the `IN` list from `?` placeholders (one per id) and pass the ids as
  arguments — never concatenate values into the SQL.
- Fewer round trips is usually the single biggest database win in a service.

units.title: Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
units.intro:
Listing results a page at a time has two common shapes. `LIMIT/OFFSET` is simple but
gets slower as the offset grows, because the database still walks the skipped rows.
Keyset pagination (`WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`) remembers the last id and jumps
straight past it. You will build both and then a keyset pager.

steps.title: OFFSET vs keyset
steps.intro:
Both approaches return a page of rows. The difference is what happens deep into the
list: OFFSET re-scans the skipped rows, keyset seeks directly using the last id.
steps.body:
## Two ways to page

```go
// OFFSET: skip the first (page*size) rows
db.Query(`SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT ? OFFSET ?`, size, page*size)

// Keyset: continue after the last id you saw
db.Query(`SELECT id FROM items WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`, lastID, size)
```

- **`LIMIT ? OFFSET ?`** is easy, but a large `OFFSET` makes the database count past
  all the skipped rows every time.
- **Keyset** carries the last id forward; with an index on `id` it seeks straight to
  the next page, so cost stays flat as you go deeper.
- Keyset needs a stable sort key (here the primary key `id`) and `ORDER BY` on it.
- The trade-off: OFFSET can jump to any page number; keyset only moves forward from a
  known row.

units.title: Indexes & EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
units.intro:
An index is a sorted structure that turns a full-table scan into a quick seek. Without
one, a `WHERE col = ?` lookup scans every row; with an index on that column, SQLite
seeks straight to the match. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows which strategy the database
chose, so you can confirm an index is actually used.

steps.title: Why indexes matter
steps.intro:
A lookup without an index is a linear SCAN. An index on the filtered column lets the
database jump to the rows it needs. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` reveals which one happens.
steps.body:
## Create an index, read the plan

```go
db.Exec(`CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email)`)

rows, _ := db.Query(`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = ?`, "a@x")
for rows.Next() {
    var id, parent, notused int
    var detail string
    rows.Scan(&id, &parent, &notused, &detail)
    // detail: "SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_users_email (email=?)"
}
```

- **`CREATE INDEX`** builds a sorted lookup structure on one or more columns.
- Without an index, the plan says **`SCAN`** — every row is examined.
- With a matching index, the plan says **`SEARCH ... USING INDEX`** — a direct seek.
- **`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`** returns rows whose last column (`detail`) is the
  human-readable strategy; read it to verify your index is doing its job.

steps.title: No index means a SCAN
steps.intro:
With no index on the filtered column, SQLite has to examine every row. `EXPLAIN QUERY
PLAN` says so — its detail text contains `SCAN`.

units.title: Goroutines & WaitGroup
units.intro:
The foundation of Go concurrency. A **goroutine** is a function that runs
concurrently, multiplexed by the Go runtime onto a small pool of OS threads — so
cheap you can launch thousands, where native threads would cost you megabytes
each. Launching one is just `go f()`. But a goroutine runs *independently*: if
`main` returns, the program ends and in-flight goroutines are dropped. A
`sync.WaitGroup` is the counter that lets `main` wait for a batch of goroutines to
finish. You will launch goroutines, coordinate them, and finish by summing a slice
across several of them — with a deterministic result.

steps.title: Goroutines vs threads, and WaitGroup
steps.intro:
Goroutines are not OS threads: the runtime schedules many goroutines onto few
threads, so they are cheap to create and switch. Because they run independently of
`main`, you need an explicit way to wait for them — that is what a WaitGroup does.
steps.body:
## Goroutines

```go
go doWork()        // runs doWork concurrently, returns immediately
go func() { ... }() // or an anonymous function, launched at once
```

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. Starting
one with `go` returns instantly; the work happens alongside the rest of your
program. The catch: when `main` returns, the whole program exits — any goroutine
still running is abandoned.

## WaitGroup: wait for a batch

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)              // one more goroutine to wait for
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()    // mark this one done on return
        work()
    }()
}
wg.Wait()                  // block until the counter reaches zero
```

Three calls do all the work: **`Add(n)`** raises the counter, **`Done()`** lowers
it by one (put it in a `defer` so it always runs), and **`Wait()`** blocks until
the counter hits zero. This is how `main` holds on until every goroutine finishes.

## Passing the loop value

When you launch a goroutine inside a loop, pass the loop value as an **argument**
so each goroutine gets its own copy:

```go
go func(n int) { use(n) }(i)
```

## A trick for lock-free results

If each goroutine writes to a **different slot** of a shared slice
(`results[i] = ...`), no two goroutines ever touch the same memory, so you need no
lock at all. You will use this to collect partial sums.

steps.title: Launch goroutines, wait with a WaitGroup
steps.intro:
Each iteration registers one goroutine with `Add(1)` and launches it; `defer
wg.Done()` marks it finished on return; `wg.Wait()` holds `main` until all three
are done, so the final line is guaranteed to print last.

Blocks until the counter hits zero — all three goroutines finished.
Prints a final line, guaranteed after every goroutine.
steps.explanation:
`Add`/`Done`/`Wait` are the whole protocol. The three worker lines may print in any
order — that is concurrency — but the final line always prints last, because
`Wait` blocks until the count returns to zero.

steps.title: Collect results without a lock

Writing to disjoint indices is the simplest safe way to gather concurrent results:

in order, because slot `i` is always written by the goroutine that owns index `i`.
