gabarito.justification:
Every element is visited exactly once across the workers, so the work is **O(n)**;
the only extra memory is one partial-sum slot per worker, a fixed count, so the
extra space is **O(1)**. Each worker owns a disjoint stride of indices and its own
output slot, so there is no shared mutable state and no lock — and because addition
is commutative, the total is identical no matter which goroutine the runtime runs
first. That is what makes the result deterministic.

units.title: Channels
units.intro:
Channels are how goroutines **communicate** — Go's motto is *"don't communicate by
sharing memory; share memory by communicating."* A channel is a typed pipe: one
goroutine sends values in, another receives them out, and the channel handles the
synchronisation. You will learn unbuffered channels (a send and a receive meet, a
rendezvous), buffered channels (a small queue), how `close` signals "no more
values", and how `range` drains a channel until it closes. The unit ends with a
producer/consumer pipeline that sums a stream of numbers.

steps.title: Sending, receiving, closing, ranging
steps.intro:
A channel carries values of one type between goroutines and synchronises them while
doing it. Unbuffered channels pair a send with a receive; buffered channels hold a
few values; closing a channel tells receivers the stream has ended.
steps.body:
## Make, send, receive

```go
ch := make(chan int)   // unbuffered channel of ints
ch <- 7                // send 7 (blocks until a receiver is ready)
v := <-ch              // receive (blocks until a value is ready)
```

On an **unbuffered** channel a send blocks until some goroutine receives, and a
receive blocks until some goroutine sends — the two meet at a single point, a
*rendezvous*. That rendezvous is itself the synchronisation.

## Buffered channels

```go
ch := make(chan int, 3)  // room for three values
ch <- 1; ch <- 2; ch <- 3 // these do not block: there is room
```

A **buffered** channel holds up to its capacity without a waiting receiver. Sends
block only when the buffer is full; receives block only when it is empty.

## Close and range

```go
close(ch)             // no more values will be sent
for v := range ch {   // yields buffered values, then stops at close
    use(v)
}

v, ok := <-ch         // ok == false once the channel is closed and drained
```

**`close`** marks a channel finished. A `range` over a channel reads values until it
is closed and drained, then ends the loop. The two-value receive `v, ok := <-ch`
reports whether a real value came (`ok` true) or the channel is closed (`ok` false).
Only the **sender** should close a channel, and never send on a closed one.

## Directional channels

A parameter typed `chan<- int` may only **send**; `<-chan int` may only **receive**.
It documents and enforces a goroutine's role.

steps.title: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous
steps.intro:
The goroutine's send blocks until `main` receives; `main`'s receive blocks until the
goroutine sends. They meet at one point — that handshake both moves the value and
synchronises the two goroutines.
steps.prompt: Send a value from a goroutine and receive it in `main` over an unbuffered channel.
line_comments: Makes an unbuffered channel of ints — a send waits for a matching receive.
Launches a goroutine, so the send has someone to pair with.
Sends 42; it blocks here until `main` receives.
Closes and calls the anonymous goroutine.
Receives from the channel — the moment the send completes, a rendezvous.
steps.explanation:
If you sent on an unbuffered channel from the only goroutine, the program would
deadlock — nobody to receive. Launching a goroutine gives the send a partner; the
two block until they meet, which is exactly how channels synchronise work.

steps.title: Buffer, close, and range
steps.intro:
A buffered channel takes three values without a receiver; `close` marks the end;
`range` then yields them in first-in-first-out order and stops cleanly at the close.
steps.prompt: Fill a buffered channel, close it, and drain it with `range` — in FIFO order.
line_comments: A buffered channel holding up to 3 ints — sends do not block while there is room.
Sends 1 into the buffer (no receiver needed yet).
Sends 3 — the buffer is now full.
`close` says no more values will be sent.
`range` over a channel yields buffered values in FIFO order, then stops at close.
Prints each value: 1, 2, 3 — always in that order.
Closes the loop (it ends when the channel is drained and closed).
steps.explanation:
Buffering lets a sender run ahead of a receiver by up to the capacity. Closing is
what lets `range` terminate — without it, the loop would block forever waiting for a
fourth value. The output order is deterministic: a channel is a FIFO queue.

steps.title: Directional channels in a pipeline
steps.intro:
The `produce` function is typed `chan<- int`, so it may only send — the compiler
enforces its role. It closes the channel when done, letting the consumer's `range`
end on its own.
steps.prompt: Write a producer that only sends, and sum its output in `main` with `range`.
line_comments: A producer function; `chan<- int` means it may only SEND on this channel.
Closes the channel so the consumer's range can stop.
Makes the channel the producer and consumer share.
A running sum on the main goroutine (the consumer).
Ranges over the channel until the producer closes it.
steps.explanation:
This is the shape of every Go pipeline: a producer sends and closes, a consumer
ranges and sums. Directional types make the roles explicit and let the compiler
catch mistakes (a producer that accidentally receives will not compile). The total
`10` is deterministic — the consumer sees every value exactly once.

steps.title: Implement SumPipeline
steps.intro:
Build a producer/consumer pipeline: one goroutine produces the numbers on a channel
and closes it; the main goroutine consumes with `range` and returns the sum. The
result is deterministic because the consumer sees every value exactly once.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SumPipeline`:

```go
func SumPipeline(nums []int) int { ... }
```

Start a goroutine that **sends** every element of `nums` on a channel and then
**closes** it. In the calling goroutine, **`range`** over the channel and return the
sum of everything you receive.

Examples:

- `SumPipeline([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})` → `15`
- `SumPipeline(nil)` → `0` (an empty producer closes immediately)

**Hint:** the producer goroutine must `close` the channel when it is done, or the
consumer's `range` will block forever.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The producer sends `n` values and the consumer receives `n` values, so the work is
**O(n)**; the unbuffered channel holds at most one in-flight value, so the extra
space is **O(1)**. Closing the channel is what lets the consumer's `range` finish.
There is exactly one sender and one receiver, so no value is seen twice — the sum is
deterministic.

units.title: Select & timeouts
units.intro:
A goroutine often has to wait on **several** channels at once, or give up after a
deadline. `select` is the tool: it blocks until one of its cases can proceed, then
runs that one. Pair it with `time.After` — a channel from the standard library that
fires after a duration — and you have timeouts. You will drain multiple channels,
add a timeout branch, and merge two closing channels into one deterministic total
using the nil-channel idiom.

steps.title: select, multiple channels, time.After
steps.intro:
`select` waits on many channel operations and proceeds with whichever is ready
first. With `time.After` you add a timeout case; with the two-value receive and a
nil channel you can drain several channels until each one closes.
steps.body:
## select

```go
select {
case v := <-a:
    useA(v)
case v := <-b:
    useB(v)
}
```

`select` blocks until **one** of its cases can run, then runs exactly that case. If
several are ready, it picks one at random — so never rely on *which* case fires,
only on the invariant you maintain (for example, a running total).

## Timeouts with time.After

```go
select {
case v := <-work:
    use(v)
case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):
    fmt.Println("timed out")
}
```

`time.After(d)` returns a `<-chan Time` that receives a value after `d` elapses.
Put it in a `select` and whichever happens first — the work or the deadline — wins.

## Draining until closed: the nil-channel idiom

A receive on a **nil** channel blocks forever, so a nil case in a `select` is simply
never chosen. That gives a clean way to merge channels until each closes:

```go
for a != nil || b != nil {
    select {
    case v, ok := <-a:
        if !ok { a = nil; continue } // closed: disable this case
        use(v)
    case v, ok := <-b:
        if !ok { b = nil; continue }
        use(v)
    }
}
```

When a channel closes, set its variable to `nil` so its case stops being selected;
the loop ends once both are nil. The *order* of arrivals varies, but a total you
accumulate does not.

steps.title: select picks whichever is ready
steps.intro:
Both channels are pre-loaded, so each `select` takes whichever one it happens to
pick first. You receive exactly two values and add them: the order select chooses
varies, but the total is fixed.
steps.prompt: Pre-load two channels and drain both with `select`, summing what you receive.
line_comments: We will receive exactly two values.
`select` waits until one of its cases is ready.
If a has a value, receive it...
If instead b is ready, receive it...
Prints 30 — the order select chooses varies, but the total does not.
steps.explanation:
`select` is the multi-way wait: it proceeds with whatever is ready. Here both cases
are ready, so Go may take either first — your code must not depend on the order,
only on the invariant (the running sum). The result `30` is deterministic.

steps.title: Add a timeout with time.After
steps.intro:
The channel is pre-loaded, so its receive is ready immediately and always wins the
`select`; the `time.After` branch is the deadline that would fire only if the value
had not arrived in time.
steps.prompt: Race a channel receive against a one-second timeout — the ready value wins.
line_comments: A buffered channel with room for one value.
Pre-load it, so the receive below is already ready.
The channel case: ready now, because we pre-loaded it.
Prints the message — this branch always wins here.
`time.After` returns a channel that fires after one second.
The timeout branch — not taken, since the value is already waiting.
steps.explanation:
`time.After` turns a deadline into just another channel, so a timeout is one more
`select` case. Because the value is already in the buffer, its case is ready at once
and always wins — a timeout only fires when the real work is too slow. No race, no
flakiness.

steps.title: Merge two channels until both close
steps.intro:
A preview of the challenge. Two goroutines feed two channels and close them. The
`select` loop drains both; when a channel closes, setting its variable to `nil`
disables that case, and the loop ends once both are nil.
steps.prompt: Merge two closing channels into one deterministic sum with the nil-channel idiom.
line_comments: ...then closes a to signal it is done.
Keep looping while either channel is still open.
`select` takes whichever channel has a value next.
Receive from a, with the two-value form to detect close.
If `ok` is false the channel is closed and drained...
...set a to nil so this case is never ready again (a nil channel blocks forever)...
Same for b: receive and detect close.
Closes the loop — both channels are now nil.
steps.explanation:
Setting a closed channel's variable to `nil` is the idiomatic way to retire a
`select` case, because a receive on nil blocks forever and so is never chosen. The
loop ends exactly when both channels have closed. Interleaving order varies; the
total `33` does not.

steps.title: Implement MergeSum
steps.intro:
Merge two streams with `select`: feed each slice on its own channel, then drain both
until each closes, summing everything. The total is deterministic even though the
interleaving of the two streams is not.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `MergeSum`:

```go
func MergeSum(a, b []int) int { ... }
```

Start one goroutine that sends every element of `a` on a channel and closes it, and
another that does the same for `b`. In the calling goroutine, use a **`select`** loop
to receive from whichever channel is ready, and return the sum of all values from
both.

Examples:

- `MergeSum([]int{1, 2, 3}, []int{10, 20})` → `36`
- `MergeSum(nil, nil)` → `0`
- `MergeSum([]int{5, 5, 5}, nil)` → `15`

**Hint:** use the two-value receive `v, ok := <-ch` to detect a closed channel, and
set that channel's variable to `nil` so its `select` case is never chosen again. Loop
while either channel is still non-nil.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Every element of both slices is received exactly once, so the work is **O(n)** in the
combined length; the two unbuffered channels hold at most one in-flight value each,
so the extra space is **O(1)**. The nil-channel idiom retires each case as its
channel closes, and the loop ends when both are nil. `select` may interleave the two
streams in any order, but summation is commutative, so the total is deterministic.

units.title: Shared state: Mutex & worker pools
units.intro:
Sometimes goroutines really must share one piece of memory — a counter, a map, an
accumulator. Then you need **mutual exclusion**: a `sync.Mutex` whose `Lock`/`Unlock`
lets only one goroutine into the critical section at a time, so updates are not
lost. For simple counters, `sync/atomic` does the same lock-free. And the canonical
way to bound concurrency is a **worker pool**: a fixed set of goroutines pulling
jobs from one channel and pushing results to another. You will guard a shared
counter, build a pool, and finish with a deterministic parallel count.

steps.title: Mutex, atomic, and the worker-pool pattern
steps.intro:
When goroutines share mutable memory, concurrent writes race and updates get lost. A
`sync.Mutex` serialises access to a critical section; `sync/atomic` does it lock-free
for single integers. A worker pool bounds how many goroutines run at once.
steps.body:
## The problem: a data race

Two goroutines running `counter++` can read the same old value and both write back
`old+1`, losing one increment. The `-race` detector flags exactly this.

## sync.Mutex

```go
var mu sync.Mutex
mu.Lock()
counter++        // critical section: exactly one goroutine at a time
mu.Unlock()
```

`Lock` blocks until the mutex is free, then this goroutine owns it; `Unlock` releases
it. Only one goroutine holds the lock at once, so the increment is safe. Keep the
critical section small, and never forget to `Unlock` (a `defer mu.Unlock()` is common).

## sync/atomic

```go
var n int64
atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)      // safe increment, no lock
total := atomic.LoadInt64(&n)
```

For a single counter, an atomic operation is simpler and faster than a mutex: the
hardware guarantees the read-modify-write happens as one indivisible step.

## Worker pool

Launch a fixed number of workers, each ranging over a shared **jobs** channel and
sending to a **results** channel:

```go
jobs := make(chan int)
results := make(chan int)
for w := 0; w < N; w++ {
    go func() {
        for j := range jobs { results <- process(j) }
    }()
}
```

Feed jobs, `close(jobs)` when done, and in a separate goroutine `wg.Wait()` then
`close(results)` so the collector's `range` can finish. A pool bounds concurrency to
`N` no matter how many jobs arrive — the standard shape for parallel work in Go.

steps.title: Guard a shared counter with a Mutex
steps.intro:
A hundred goroutines increment one shared counter. The mutex makes each increment a
critical section entered by one goroutine at a time, so no update is lost — the
result is exactly 100.
steps.prompt: Increment a shared counter from 100 goroutines, protected by a `sync.Mutex`.
line_comments: A mutex: only one goroutine may hold its lock at a time.
The shared counter every goroutine will increment.
A WaitGroup to wait for all 100 goroutines.
Takes the lock — any other goroutine must wait here.
The critical section: increment the shared counter safely.
Releases the lock so the next goroutine can proceed.
Prints 100 — the lock makes the result deterministic (no lost updates).
steps.explanation:
Without the lock, concurrent `counter++` would race and you would usually see fewer
than 100. The mutex serialises the critical section, so every increment lands. Run
it under `go run -race .` and the detector stays silent — the lock removed the race.

steps.title: Build a worker pool
steps.intro:
Three workers pull jobs from one channel and push squares to another. A separate
goroutine waits for the workers and closes the results channel, so the collector's
`range` ends cleanly. The total is the same no matter which worker handled which job.
steps.prompt: Square five numbers with a three-worker pool and sum the results.
line_comments: The jobs channel: work waiting to be done.
The results channel: finished work coming back.
A WaitGroup to know when all workers are done.
Starts three worker goroutines — the pool.
A worker pulls jobs until the channel is closed and drained.
Does the work (square it) and sends the result.
The main goroutine feeds five jobs...
...one at a time into the jobs channel.
`close(jobs)` tells the workers no more jobs are coming.
...then closes results so the collector below can stop.
Ranges over results until it is closed.
Prints 55 = 1+4+9+16+25 — deterministic regardless of which worker did which job.
steps.explanation:
The pool bounds concurrency to three workers however many jobs arrive. Closing
`jobs` ends each worker's `range`; a separate goroutine waits for them all, then
closes `results` so the collector can finish. The total `55` is deterministic: every
job is processed exactly once and addition does not care about order.

steps.title: A lock-free counter with sync/atomic
steps.intro:
For a single integer counter, `sync/atomic` is simpler than a mutex: the add is one
indivisible hardware operation, so fifty goroutines produce exactly 50 with no lock
and no race.
steps.prompt: Count to 50 across goroutines using `atomic.AddInt64` instead of a mutex.
line_comments: An int64 counter — `atomic` operates on sized integers.
`atomic.AddInt64` increments safely without a mutex — one indivisible operation.
Reads the counter atomically and prints 50.
steps.explanation:
Atomics are the lightest tool for a single shared counter: no lock to acquire, just a
hardware-level read-modify-write. For anything more than one value (a map, several
fields updated together) reach back for a `sync.Mutex`. Either way the result here is
a deterministic 50, and `-race` stays silent.

steps.title: Implement ParallelCount
steps.intro:
Finish the track with the worker-pool pattern: dispatch the numbers to a fixed set
of workers over a jobs channel, have them report over a results channel, and return
how many are even. Bounded concurrency, deterministic total.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `ParallelCount`:

```go
func ParallelCount(nums []int) int { ... }
```

Using a **worker pool** (a fixed number of goroutines reading from a shared jobs
channel and writing to a results channel), return how many values in `nums` are
**even**. The answer must be deterministic regardless of scheduling.

Examples:

- `ParallelCount([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6})` → `3`
- `ParallelCount(nil)` → `0`
- `ParallelCount([]int{1, 3, 5, 7})` → `0`

**Hint:** start N workers that `range` over the jobs channel; feed the numbers and
`close(jobs)`; in a separate goroutine `wg.Wait()` then `close(results)`; sum the
results (1 for even, 0 for odd) on the calling goroutine.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n` numbers is processed once by some worker and produces one result, so
the work is **O(n)**; the pool is a fixed number of workers with unbuffered channels,
so the extra space is **O(1)** (independent of `n`). The pool bounds concurrency, the
closer goroutine ends the results stream after every worker finishes, and because the
count is a sum of 0/1 flags, it is identical no matter which worker handled which
number — deterministic.

units.title: Stacks & queues with slices
units.intro:
Two of the most useful data structures need no library at all — a Go slice is enough.
Push and pop from the right and a slice behaves as a **stack** (last in, first out);
take from the front instead and it is a **queue** (first in, first out). You will build
both, use a stack to reverse a slice, and finish by checking bracket balance — the
canonical stack problem.

steps.title: A slice is a stack and a queue
steps.intro:
`append` grows a slice on the right; reslicing shrinks it. Pop the right end and you have
a LIFO stack; take the left end and you have a FIFO queue. No container package required.
steps.body:
## Stack (LIFO)

Push with `append`, peek the last element, pop by reslicing away the last element:

```go
stack = append(stack, x)      // push
top := stack[len(stack)-1]    // peek the top
stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]  // pop
```

Last in, first out: the most recent push is the first pop.

## Queue (FIFO)

Push on the right, but take from the **front**:

```go
queue = append(queue, x)  // enqueue
front := queue[0]         // peek the front
queue = queue[1:]         // dequeue
```

First in, first out: the oldest element leaves first.

## When to reach for what

A stack models "undo", recursion, and matching brackets. A queue models work waiting in
line and breadth-first traversal. Reslicing is O(1), so both are cheap. (Reslicing a
queue's front repeatedly keeps the dropped heads in the backing array; for long-lived
queues use a ring buffer or `container/list`. For exercises, a slice is perfect.)

steps.title: Push and pop a stack
steps.intro:
Push three values onto a slice-stack, then pop one. Because the last value pushed is the
first popped, the result is fully deterministic.
steps.prompt:
Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop the top.

**Why:** a stack is the simplest use of `append`/reslice, and its last-in-first-out order
is the backbone of bracket matching, undo stacks, and depth-first traversal.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    stack := []int{}
    stack = append(stack, 1)
    stack = append(stack, 2)
    stack = append(stack, 3)
    top := stack[len(stack)-1]
    stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]
    fmt.Println("popped", top, "left", stack)
}
line_comments: An empty int slice used as a stack.
Push 1 — `append` grows the slice on the right (the top).
Push 3 on top — the stack is now [1 2 3].
Peek the top: the last element.
Pop: reslice to drop the last element (LIFO).
Prints `popped 3 left [1 2]` — last in, first out.
steps.explanation:
The top of a slice-stack is its last element, so peeking is `stack[len(stack)-1]` and
popping is `stack[:len(stack)-1]`. Push 1, 2, 3 and the top is 3 — the most recent push
is the first pop. Deterministic every run.

steps.title: Enqueue and dequeue a queue
steps.intro:
Enqueue three strings on the right, then dequeue from the front. First in, first out — the
oldest value leaves first, so the output never varies.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    queue := []string{}
    queue = append(queue, "a")
    queue = append(queue, "b")
    queue = append(queue, "c")
    front := queue[0]
    queue = queue[1:]
    fmt.Println("served", front, "left", queue)
}
line_comments: An empty string slice used as a queue.
Enqueue "c" — the queue is now [a b c].
Peek the front: the first element.
Dequeue: reslice to drop the first element (FIFO).
Prints `served a left [b c]` — first in, first out.
steps.explanation:
A queue removes from the front: peek is `queue[0]`, dequeue is `queue[1:]`. The first value
enqueued ("a") is the first served, so FIFO order makes the output deterministic.

steps.title: Reverse a slice with a stack
steps.intro:
Push every value onto a stack, then pop them all. Popping yields the values in reverse
order — a stack is a reversing machine.
steps.prompt:
Reverse [1 2 3 4] by pushing each value, then popping all.

**Why:** reversal falls out of LIFO for free; the same push-then-drain idea powers
depth-first traversal and expression evaluation.
line_comments: Walk the input left to right...
While the stack is not empty...
steps.explanation:
Pushing 1,2,3,4 and then popping gives 4,3,2,1: the last pushed is the first popped. Draining
a stack into a new slice reverses it, with no index arithmetic and no extra copy.

steps.title: Implement BalancedParens
steps.intro:
The classic stack problem: decide whether a string of brackets is balanced. Push each
opener; on a closer, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. Empty stack at the
end means balanced.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `BalancedParens`:

```go
func BalancedParens(s string) bool { ... }
```

Return `true` when every bracket in `s` is closed in the correct order, considering the
three pairs `()`, `[]` and `{}`. Any other character should be ignored.

Examples:

- `BalancedParens("")` -> `true`
- `BalancedParens("()[]{}")` -> `true`
- `BalancedParens("([{}])")` -> `true`
- `BalancedParens("(]")` -> `false`
- `BalancedParens(")(")` -> `false`

**Hint:** keep a stack of open brackets. Push every opener. On a closer, fail if the stack
is empty or its top is not the matching opener; otherwise pop. At the end, balanced means
the stack is empty.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each character is visited once, so the scan is **O(n)**; the stack holds at most one entry
per unmatched opener, so worst-case space is **O(n)**. A closer is legal only when the stack
top is its matching opener — otherwise the string is unbalanced. Leftover openers at the end
(non-empty stack) also mean unbalanced. Non-bracket characters hit no `switch` case and are
ignored.

units.title: Singly linked lists
units.intro:
A linked list stores each value in its own node that points to the next one. Unlike a
slice, there is no contiguous block — just pointers hopping from node to node. You will
define a `Node`, push to the front, pop from the front, measure length, and finish by
reversing a slice through a list.

steps.title: Nodes and pointers
steps.intro:
A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. A `nil` next marks the end. The list
itself is just a pointer to the first node — the head.
steps.body:
## The node

```go
type Node struct {
    Val  int
    Next *Node
}
```

`Next` is a pointer; `nil` means "no next node". An empty list is a `nil` head.

## Push to the front

Make a new node whose `Next` is the current head, then move the head to it — O(1):

```go
head = &Node{Val: v, Next: head}
```

## Walk the list

Follow `Next` from the head until you reach `nil`:

```go
for n := head; n != nil; n = n.Next {
    use(n.Val)
}
```

Pushing to the front is cheap and reverses insertion order: the last value pushed is the
first one you meet when walking. Popping the front is just `head = head.Next`. That front
bias is exactly what makes a linked list a natural reversing tool.

steps.title: Build a list by pushing to the front
steps.intro:
Push 1, 2, 3 to the front of a list, then walk it. Because each push lands in front, the
walk sees them newest-first — a deterministic 3 2 1.
steps.prompt:
Push 1, 2, 3 to the front of a linked list and print the values.

**Why:** front insertion is the O(1) building block of linked lists, and it naturally
reverses the order you insert in.
line_comments: ...and a pointer to the next node (nil at the end).
An empty list is just a nil head pointer.
Push 1 to the front: a node whose Next is the old head.
Push 3 to the front — head now points at 3.
Walk from head following Next until nil.
steps.explanation:
Each `&Node{Val: v, Next: head}` splices a new node in front of the current head, then head
moves to it. Pushing 1,2,3 leaves the list 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> nil, so the walk prints `3 2 1`.

steps.title: Pop the front of a list
steps.intro:
Remove the first node by moving the head to the second node. The popped value and the new
head are both fixed, so the output is deterministic.
steps.prompt:
Pop the front node of a two-node list and show the new head.

**Why:** popping the front is just `head = head.Next` — O(1), and the mirror image of
pushing to the front.
line_comments: Remember the front value before removing it.
Pop the front: move head to the second node.
steps.explanation:
Popping the front keeps a copy of `head.Val`, then advances `head` to `head.Next`. The old
first node is now unreferenced (garbage collected). New head is 20 — deterministic.

steps.title: Measure a list's length
steps.intro:
Count the nodes by walking from head to nil, one tick per node. A three-node list has
length 3, every time.
steps.prompt:
Count the nodes in a three-node list.

**Why:** length is O(n) for a linked list — there is no stored size, so you must walk it.
That walk is the template for every list operation.
line_comments: `length` counts the nodes starting at head.
steps.explanation:
A linked list stores no size, so length means walking from head to `nil` and counting. Three
nodes give `length = 3`. The same head-to-nil walk underpins search, print, and reverse.

steps.title: Implement ReverseList
steps.intro:
Put front insertion to work: push every input value onto the front of a list, then walk the
list collecting values. Because front insertion reverses order, you get the input reversed —
without indexing from the back.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `ReverseList`:

```go
func ReverseList(items []int) []int { ... }
```

Build a singly linked list by pushing each value of `items` onto the **front**, then walk
the list from head to `nil` collecting the values into a new slice. The result is `items`
reversed.

Examples:

- `ReverseList(nil)` -> `[]`
- `ReverseList([]int{1})` -> `[1]`
- `ReverseList([]int{1, 2, 3})` -> `[3 2 1]`

**Hint:** start with a `nil` head. For each `v`, do `head = &Node{Val: v, Next: head}`.
Then walk `head` collecting `n.Val` into a slice and return it.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each value is pushed once (**O(n)**) and the list holds one node per value (**O(n)** space).
Front insertion builds the list in reverse: the last value pushed becomes the head, so
walking head-to-nil yields the input reversed. Pre-sizing `out` with `make(..., 0, len)`
avoids re-allocations during the collecting walk.

units.title: Maps, frequencies & sets
units.intro:
A `map` gives you O(1) average lookup by key — the engine behind counting, grouping, de-
duplication and membership tests. You will count frequencies, model a **set** with
`map[int]struct{}`, test membership with the comma-ok idiom, and finish with Two Sum, where
a map turns a quadratic scan into a single pass. One rule throughout: map iteration order is
randomised, so sort keys before printing.

steps.title: Counting, sets, and deterministic output
steps.intro:
`map[K]V` indexes values by key. A missing key reads as the zero value, so `m[k]++` counts
without initialising. A set is a map whose value carries no data: `map[K]struct{}`.
steps.body:
## Frequency counting

A missing key yields the zero value, so incrementing just works:

```go
freq := map[string]int{}
freq[word]++     // starts at 0 for a new word
```

## Sets with the empty struct

`struct{}{}` is a value that occupies zero bytes — perfect as a set's payload:

```go
set := map[int]struct{}{}
set[x] = struct{}{}          // add
_, ok := set[x]              // membership (comma-ok)
```

## The comma-ok idiom

Indexing a map returns an optional second boolean: `v, ok := m[k]`. `ok` is `true` only
when the key is present, which distinguishes "absent" from "present but zero".

## Determinism

**Map iteration order is randomised by design.** Never print a map directly if order
matters. Collect the keys, `sort` them, then iterate:

```go
keys := make([]string, 0, len(freq))
for k := range freq { keys = append(keys, k) }
sort.Strings(keys)
```

That one habit keeps map-derived output reproducible run after run.

steps.title: Count word frequencies
steps.intro:
Tally how often each word appears, then print the counts in sorted key order. Sorting the
keys first makes the output deterministic despite random map iteration.
steps.prompt:
Count the words in a slice and print each word with its count, sorted.

**Why:** `m[k]++` is the idiomatic counter, and sorting keys before printing is the fix for
Go's deliberately randomised map iteration.
line_comments: A map from word to its count.
...increment its count (missing keys start at zero).
Collect the map keys into a slice.
Map iteration order is random, so gather the keys...
Sort the keys so the output is deterministic.
Walk the keys in sorted order...
steps.explanation:
`freq[w]++` relies on a missing key reading as 0, so no initialisation is needed. The map
itself has no stable order, so we collect the keys, `sort.Strings` them, and print in that
order — giving the fixed output `go 3` then `rust 2`.

steps.title: De-duplicate with a set
steps.intro:
Insert every value into a `map[int]struct{}`; duplicates collapse to a single key. Collect
the keys, sort them, and the distinct values print in a fixed order.
steps.prompt:
Remove duplicates from a slice using a set, then print the sorted unique values.

**Why:** `map[int]struct{}` is the idiomatic Go set — zero-byte values, O(1) membership —
and the natural tool for de-duplication.
line_comments: A set: a map whose value is the empty struct (zero bytes).
...add it to the set — duplicates collapse to one key.
steps.explanation:
Writing `set[n] = struct{}{}` records membership using a value that costs zero bytes. Repeated
numbers overwrite the same key, so the set holds each value once. Sorting before printing
turns the unordered set into the fixed output `[1 2 3]`.

steps.title: Test membership with comma-ok
steps.intro:
Build a set of permissions and ask whether two keys are present. The comma-ok form returns a
boolean that is deterministic: `read` is in, `exec` is out.
steps.prompt:
Check whether `read` and `exec` belong to a permission set.

**Why:** the comma-ok idiom (`_, ok := m[k]`) is how Go distinguishes "present" from
"absent", the heart of every set-membership test.
line_comments: ...`read` is present ({} is the empty struct value)...
Comma-ok membership test: is `read` in the set?
Is `exec` in the set? (it is not).
steps.explanation:
Indexing a map yields an optional second value: `_, ok := m[k]` sets `ok` to `true` only when
the key exists. `read` was added, so `canRead` is true; `exec` was never added, so `canExec`
is false. The literal `{}` is shorthand for `struct{}{}` inside the map.

steps.title: Implement TwoSum
steps.intro:
Two Sum is the canonical map problem: find two indices whose values add up to a target. A
map of value->index lets you check for the needed complement in O(1), turning a nested-loop
O(n^2) search into a single O(n) pass.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `TwoSum`:

```go
func TwoSum(nums []int, target int) (int, int, bool) { ... }
```

Return indices `i < j` such that `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, with the smaller index
first, and a boolean reporting whether such a pair was found. Return the **first** such pair
in scan order. If no pair exists, return `0, 0, false`.

Examples:

- `TwoSum([]int{2, 7, 11, 15}, 9)` -> `0, 1, true`
- `TwoSum([]int{3, 2, 4}, 6)` -> `1, 2, true`
- `TwoSum([]int{3, 3}, 6)` -> `0, 1, true`
- `TwoSum([]int{1, 2, 3}, 100)` -> `0, 0, false`

**Hint:** scan with index `j`. Keep a map `seen` from value to its earliest index. If
`target - nums[j]` is already in `seen`, you have your pair (its stored index, then `j`).
Otherwise store `nums[j]` and continue.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
One pass over `nums` (**O(n)**) with a map holding at most one index per value (**O(n)**
space). For each `v` at index `j`, the complement `target - v` is looked up in O(1); if it was
seen earlier its stored index is smaller than `j`, so returning `(i, j)` gives the smaller
index first. Storing only the first occurrence of each value keeps `i` minimal. Finding the
complement before inserting `v` prevents using one element twice.

units.title: Binary search trees
units.intro:
A binary search tree keeps its values ordered: every node's left subtree holds smaller
values, its right subtree larger ones. That invariant makes lookup and ordered traversal
fall out naturally. You will build a tree, insert recursively, search it, walk it in order
(which yields sorted values), and finish by turning a bag of inserts into a sorted slice.

steps.title: The ordering invariant
steps.intro:
A BST node has a value and two children. The invariant: everything in the left subtree is
smaller than the node, everything in the right is larger. Keep it, and the tree stays sorted.

steps.title: Build a tree by hand
steps.intro:
Wire a root with a smaller left child and a larger right child. Reading the three values back
shows the ordering invariant directly.
steps.prompt:
Make a root holding 5, a left child 3, and a right child 8; print all three.

**Why:** seeing left < root < right by hand makes the BST invariant concrete before any
recursion enters the picture.
line_comments: Smaller value 3 goes on the left.
Larger value 8 goes on the right.
steps.explanation:
The invariant is just left < root < right. Placing 3 on the left of 5 and 8 on the right
satisfies it, and reading `root.Val`, `root.Left.Val`, `root.Right.Val` prints `5 3 8`.

steps.title: Insert recursively
steps.intro:
Insert 5, 3, 8 into an empty tree with a recursive helper that returns the subtree root. The
resulting shape — 5 at the root, 3 left, 8 right — is fixed.
steps.prompt:
Insert 5, 3, 8 into an empty BST and print root, left, right.

**Why:** the return-the-root recursion (`root.Left = insert(root.Left, v)`) is the standard,
nil-safe way to grow a tree, handling the empty tree and every subtree the same way.
line_comments: An empty spot: create the node here.
Prints `5 3 8` — 5 at the root, 3 left, 8 right.
steps.explanation:
`insert` returns the subtree root, so `root = insert(root, v)` handles the empty tree (returns
a fresh node) and deeper subtrees uniformly. Inserting 5 then 3 then 8 builds 5 with 3 on the
left and 8 on the right, printing `5 3 8`.

steps.title: In-order traversal is sorted
steps.intro:
Walk left, node, right and collect the values. For a BST this emits them ascending, so the
small tree 5/3/8 prints as [3 5 8].
steps.prompt:
Collect the in-order traversal of a 5/3/8 tree into a slice.

**Why:** in-order traversal of a BST is exactly a sorted walk — the property that makes a
tree double as an ordering structure.
line_comments: Nothing to do for an empty subtree...
Visit the left subtree first (smaller values).
Then visit the right subtree (larger values).
The slice that will collect the traversal.
Prints `[3 5 8]` — in-order of a BST is sorted.
steps.explanation:
Visiting left subtree, then node, then right subtree yields values in ascending order for any
BST. The pointer-to-slice parameter lets each recursive call append to the same `out`. The
5/3/8 tree prints `[3 5 8]`.

steps.title: Implement SortedFromInserts
steps.intro:
Combine insert and in-order traversal: feed every item into a BST, then read it back in
order. Duplicates are ignored by the tree, so you get the distinct values, sorted — a tiny
tree-sort.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SortedFromInserts`:

```go
func SortedFromInserts(items []int) []int { ... }
```

Insert every value of `items` into a binary search tree, then return the in-order traversal.
The result must be sorted ascending, with **duplicates removed** (a repeated value is only
stored once by the tree).

Examples:

- `SortedFromInserts(nil)` -> `[]`
- `SortedFromInserts([]int{5, 3, 8, 1, 4})` -> `[1 3 4 5 8]`
- `SortedFromInserts([]int{5, 1, 5, 3, 1})` -> `[1 3 5]`
- `SortedFromInserts([]int{3, 3, 3})` -> `[3]`

**Hint:** reuse the recursive `insert` (ignore a value equal to the current node) and the
`inorder` walk from the drills. Insert all items, traverse into a slice, return it.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each insert costs the tree's height — **O(log n)** on average over `n` items, so building is
**O(n log n)**; the traversal is O(n). Space is **O(n)** for the nodes. Insert ignores a value
equal to the current node, so duplicates never enter the tree, and in-order traversal of a BST
is sorted — giving distinct, ascending output. `out` starts as `[]int{}` so an empty input
returns a non-nil empty slice.

units.title: Sorting & searching by hand
units.intro:
The standard library can sort for you, but knowing how is the point here. You will write
binary search on a sorted slice, merge two sorted runs into one, sort in place with insertion
sort, and finish by implementing **merge sort** end to end — a new sorted slice with no help
from the `sort` package.

steps.title: Divide, merge, and search
steps.intro:
Binary search halves a sorted range each step — O(log n). Merge sort splits a slice in two,
sorts each half, and merges them back — O(n log n). Both are built from simple index work.
steps.body:
## Binary search

On a sorted slice, compare the middle and discard half each iteration:

```go
lo, hi := 0, len(v)-1
for lo <= hi {
    mid := (lo + hi) / 2
    if v[mid] == target { return mid }
    if v[mid] < target { lo = mid + 1 } else { hi = mid - 1 }
}
return -1
```

## Merge

Combine two sorted slices by always taking the smaller front element:

```go
for i < len(a) && j < len(b) {
    if a[i] <= b[j] { out = append(out, a[i]); i++ } else { out = append(out, b[j]); j++ }
}
out = append(out, a[i:]...)   // drain the rest
out = append(out, b[j:]...)
```

## Merge sort

Split, recurse, merge:

```go
mid := len(v) / 2
left := MergeSort(v[:mid])
right := MergeSort(v[mid:])
return merge(left, right)
```

A slice of length 0 or 1 is already sorted — that is the base case. Using `<=` in the merge
keeps equal elements in their original relative order, so merge sort is **stable**.

steps.title: Binary search a sorted slice
steps.intro:
Search a sorted slice by repeatedly halving the range. A present value returns its index; an
absent one returns -1 — both deterministic.
steps.prompt:
Find 7 (present) and 4 (absent) in a sorted slice with binary search.

**Why:** binary search is the payoff for keeping data sorted — O(log n) lookups instead of a
linear scan, using nothing but index arithmetic.
line_comments: `search` finds target in a sorted slice, or returns -1.
Prints `3 -1` — 7 is at index 3, 4 is absent.
steps.explanation:
Each iteration compares the midpoint and throws away half the range, so the search is O(log n).
7 sits at index 3; 4 is never found, so the loop exits and returns -1. Output: `3 -1`.

steps.title: Merge two sorted slices
steps.intro:
Walk two sorted slices with a cursor each, always taking the smaller front value, then drain
whatever remains. The merged slice is one sorted run.
steps.prompt:
Merge [1 4 7] and [2 3 8] into one sorted slice.

**Why:** merging two sorted runs in linear time is the engine of merge sort — and of any
external sort that cannot fit data in memory.
line_comments: `merge` combines two sorted slices into one sorted slice.
Two read cursors, one per input.
While both inputs still have elements...
Prints `[1 2 3 4 7 8]` — one sorted run from two.
steps.explanation:
With both inputs already sorted, the smaller of the two front elements is the next output
element. When one input empties, the rest of the other is appended wholesale. `<=` keeps equal
elements stable. Merging [1 4 7] and [2 3 8] gives `[1 2 3 4 7 8]`.

steps.title: Insertion sort in place
steps.intro:
Grow a sorted prefix one element at a time: lift each value out and slide larger neighbours
right until it drops into place. The slice ends up sorted ascending.
steps.prompt:
Sort [4 2 5 1 3] in place with insertion sort.

**Why:** insertion sort is the simplest in-place sort and the base case many hybrid sorts fall
back to for small inputs — worth writing once by hand.
line_comments: Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix one element at a time.
The element to place into the sorted prefix.
Start comparing just left of it.
While the left neighbour is larger than the key...
...shift it one slot to the right...
Drop the key into the open slot.
Prints `[1 2 3 4 5]` — sorted by hand, no `sort` package.
steps.explanation:
Everything left of `i` is kept sorted. Each new `key` slides past the larger elements (shifting
them right) until it reaches its slot. After the pass, the slice is fully sorted: `[1 2 3 4 5]`.

steps.title: Implement MergeSort
steps.intro:
Put divide-and-conquer together: split the slice, sort each half recursively, and merge the
halves. Return a brand-new sorted slice — and leave the input untouched — without calling the
`sort` package.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `MergeSort`:

```go
func MergeSort(v []int) []int { ... }
```

Return a **new** slice with `v`'s values in ascending order. You may **not** use the `sort`
package. The input slice must be left unmodified, and duplicates must be preserved.

Examples:

- `MergeSort(nil)` -> `[]`
- `MergeSort([]int{42})` -> `[42]`
- `MergeSort([]int{5, 4, 3, 2, 1})` -> `[1 2 3 4 5]`
- `MergeSort([]int{3, 1, 2, 3, 1})` -> `[1 1 2 3 3]`

**Hint:** base case — a slice of length 0 or 1 is already sorted, so return a copy. Otherwise
split at `len(v)/2`, recurse on each half, and merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly
taking the smaller front element.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The slice is halved log n times and each level does O(n) merging, so the total is
**O(n log n)**; the merged outputs use **O(n)** extra space. The base case copies the 0- or
1-element slice, so a fresh slice is always returned and the input is never mutated. `merge`
uses `<=`, keeping equal elements in order — a stable sort — and duplicates are preserved.

units.title: Recursion & dynamic programming
units.intro:
Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller versions of itself. When those subproblems
overlap, plain recursion redoes the same work exponentially — and **dynamic programming** fixes
it by solving each subproblem once and storing the answer. You will write classic recursions,
watch naive Fibonacci blow up, rebuild it bottom-up, and finish with the coin-change problem.

steps.title: From recursion to memoized DP
steps.intro:
A recursive function needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (how to shrink the
problem). When subproblems repeat, caching their results — dynamic programming — removes the
exponential blow-up.

steps.title: Factorial by recursion
steps.intro:
Factorial is the gentlest recursion: a base case at 1 and a single smaller call. The answer
for 5 is a fixed 120.
steps.prompt:
Compute 5! recursively.

**Why:** factorial shows the two essential parts of any recursion — a base case to stop and a
recursive case that shrinks the input — with no overlap to worry about.
steps.explanation:
`fact` stops at `n <= 1` (the base case) and otherwise multiplies `n` by `fact(n-1)`. Unwinding
5*4*3*2*1 gives 120. No subproblem repeats, so plain recursion is already efficient here.

steps.title: Naive recursive Fibonacci
steps.intro:
Fibonacci branches into two recursive calls, which recompute the same values repeatedly. It
still returns the right answer (fib(10) = 55) — just with wasteful, exponential work.
steps.prompt:
Compute fib(10) with the naive two-branch recursion.

**Why:** this is the textbook example of overlapping subproblems — correct but exponential —
and the motivation for dynamic programming in the next drill.
line_comments: `fib` computes the nth Fibonacci number naively.
Recursive case — recomputes overlapping subproblems (exponential work).
steps.explanation:
Each call spawns two more, and the same `fib(k)` is recomputed across branches, so the work
grows exponentially. The result is correct — fib(10) = 55 — but the method is wasteful, which
is exactly what dynamic programming repairs.

steps.title: Fibonacci with bottom-up DP
steps.intro:
Fill a table from the bottom up: each entry is the sum of the two before it, computed once.
Same answer as the naive version — fib(10) = 55 — in linear time.
steps.prompt:
Compute fib(10) by filling a DP table from the bottom up.

**Why:** solving each subproblem once and storing it turns the exponential recursion into a
single linear pass — the core idea of dynamic programming.
line_comments: `fib` computes the nth Fibonacci number with bottom-up DP.
Fill the table from the bottom up...
...each entry is the sum of the two before it (each solved once).
The answer is the last table entry.
Prints `55` — same result as the naive version, far less work.
steps.explanation:
The table `dp` stores each Fibonacci number once, smallest first, so `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]`
never recomputes. The guard handles small `n` safely. fib(10) is `dp[10] = 55`, in O(n) time
and O(n) space instead of exponential.

steps.title: Implement CoinChange
steps.intro:
The coin-change problem is a dynamic-programming classic: given coin denominations, make an
amount using as few coins as possible. Build the answer bottom-up, one amount at a time, and
report -1 when the amount cannot be made.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `CoinChange`:

```go
func CoinChange(coins []int, amount int) int { ... }
```

Return the **fewest** coins from `coins` (each usable any number of times) that sum exactly to
`amount`, or `-1` if it cannot be made. `amount` 0 needs 0 coins.

Examples:

- `CoinChange([]int{1, 2, 5}, 11)` -> `3`  (5 + 5 + 1)
- `CoinChange([]int{2}, 3)` -> `-1`
- `CoinChange([]int{1, 2, 5}, 0)` -> `0`
- `CoinChange([]int{1, 3, 4}, 6)` -> `2`  (3 + 3, not 4 + 1 + 1)

**Hint:** let `dp[x]` be the fewest coins for amount `x`, with `dp[0] = 0` and every other
entry starting at "infinity". For each `x` from 1 to `amount`, try every coin `c <= x`:
`dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x-c] + 1)`. If `dp[amount]` is still infinite, return -1.

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
`dp[x]` is the fewest coins for amount `x`. The outer loop runs `amount` times, the inner over
every coin, giving **O(amount * len(coins))** time and **O(amount)** space. Each `dp[x]` is
built from already-solved smaller amounts (`dp[x-c]`), so a bottom-up pass fills the table once.
`dp[0]` stays 0 (base case), and an entry still at infinity means that amount is unreachable, so
`dp[amount]` infinite returns -1. Trying every coin — not the largest greedily — is what makes
`[1 3 4]` for 6 yield 2 (3+3) rather than 3.
